text: Hierarchical navigable small world graphs approximate nearest neighbour search by walking a layered proximity graph, trading recall for latency.
Inverted file indexes partition the vector space into Voronoi cells and search only the cells nearest the query centroid.
Product quantization compresses vectors by splitting them into subvectors and replacing each with a codebook entry, shrinking memory at the cost of precision.
Exact k nearest neighbour search computes every dot product and keeps the best k, which guarantees perfect recall by construction.
A matrix vector product over a million rows of 768 dimensional float32 streams about three gigabytes, so exact search is memory bandwidth bound rather than compute bound.
Metadata filtering with a boolean mask applied before the dot products is exact, and gets cheaper as the filter becomes more selective.
The manifest records the embedder identity so that opening an index with a different model fails loudly instead of returning meaningless rankings.
Vectors are stored little endian because the JVM defaults to big endian and an unstated byte order is a silent corruption waiting to happen.
Deleting a row sets a bit in a bitmap rather than rewriting the matrix, so updates are append only and cost nothing until compaction.
An offset table turns fetching a document for a search result into a seek and a read of known length instead of a scan of the whole file.
Document and query embeddings use different task types, and collapsing them into a single call is a silent retrieval quality loss.
Normalising every row at write time makes cosine similarity a plain dot product and makes the index immune to a model that changes its output convention.
Truncating an embedding to fewer dimensions saves storage but only some models renormalise the truncated output.

Reciprocal rank fusion combines two ranked lists using only ranks, so no score calibration between the systems is needed.
